chapter: Corrections and views on early Black music
title: Sidney Bechet, William Marion Cook, Mary Wayne and Eugene Michael
summary: The two discuss Bechet's trip with Cook, then White praises Cook, Mary Wayne's orchestra and his teacher Eugene Michael over Europe.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: Sidney Bechet was over there about the time of the war, too.
Yeah. No, not World War I.
I thought he went over around 1918 or 1902. I don't think he was in the service.
No, he was not in the service. I think he went over with William Marion Cook's band.

And they might have introduced a sort of a modern aspect of a little ragtime with an interruption by him. But Sidney himself could not play qualifiedly in William Marion Cook's band at that time. No, he wasn't a good band.

I know William Marion Cook personally. I knew it. Fine pianist, fine arranging, fine violinist, and a scat if you just commit one error in his music, especially in the pit. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. You see? And then there were other things about the Negro and ragtime and jazz which a few writers have disqualified, but not so. You see, the top orchestra in New York at that time was Mary Wayne and Mary Anderson and Mary Lucas because they could go to the Union and resurrect 25 pieces of hair for an occasion right out of the Union. The finest orchestra I ever heard in New York was conducted by a Negro woman, Mary Wayne. And every musician in there looked at me. They couldn't talk English because I went to the bar myself. I sneaked out of the Jacob's office band and went. And she was up there with her violin conducting. And as for band masters, I don't think no band master ever talked to Eugene Michael. I'm not saying it because he's my teacher. But you see, he personally conducted Europe's band on any intimate concert occasion where there was an official officer to arrive. You see, because Europe was a scrambling trombone player, brow beating the horn, and plunking the piano. Now, as for being an arranger of music and a musician, he was not that. But Eugene Michael was polished. You see, the man had held his seat of instructor of music. I mean the entire music department at Tuskegee. He is a graduate of Clapton University in Orangeburg, South Carolina. And one of the second teachers in the Jenkins office. That was Eugene Michael. And then he founded the Michael School of Music on Long Island in New York, Aticella. He's dead now. He has sons in New York. And if you ever go to New York to get an interview from him, find his sons and go look through that library, you'll find the Jenkins office band on his walls out there. And it's great. So contrary to some people's opinions about that, like Duke Ellington wrote in a magazine said prior to 1915 there were no Negro reading pianists. What are you going to do with him?
